body.text: Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s first official visit to India produced more than diplomatic symbolism. New Delhi announced a large reconstruction and development package, committed to new energy and transit initiatives, and joined Kathmandu in adopting a broad vision for a more modern bilateral relationship.

Shah sought to signal a different governing style after the 2025 Gen Z protests, which reflected impatience with slow delivery and political symbolism. His roughly 25-hour, New Delhi-only visit – focused on meetings with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, President Droupadi Murmu, and External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar – was therefore an early test of whether his government can turn its results-oriented message into tangible diplomatic gains.

India committed about $1.62 billion in development assistance. This includes approximately $378 million in grants for post-disaster reconstruction and infrastructure, and a $1.24 billion rupee-denominated line of credit for energy projects.

The package is especially important after the Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi floods, which damaged infrastructure and disrupted Nepal’s principal land route to China. But it should be viewed in proportion. Nepal’s preliminary reconstruction and recovery needs are estimated at roughly $4.89 billion, according to the Nepal’s Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment. Even if the full Indian package is realized, it would cover only a portion of those needs, and much of it is an energy line of credit rather than reconstruction grant assistance.

The clearest strategic gain was in energy, where Nepal’s economic opportunity depends increasingly on transmission capacity and dependable access to the Indian market. The two countries laid the foundation stone for the 669-megawatt Lower Arun hydroelectric project and welcomed progress toward joint ventures for two high-capacity transmission lines: Inaruwa-New Purnea and Dododhara-Bareilly.

Nepal’s future electricity exports depend not simply on building more hydropower plants. Nepal will need cross-border transmission capacity, predictable market access, and Indian regulatory approval. Kathmandu has now secured authorization to sell roughly 1,200 megawatts in the Indian market during periods of surplus generation, according to recent reporting on approvals. Yet it must still import power during the dry season, especially after flood damage reduced domestic generation. That contrast illustrates why transmission and dependable market access may matter more than another generic endorsement of power trade.

In terms of connectivity, India opened a new transit avenue through Deendayal port at Kandla and indicated that access to Paradip port could follow once the necessary infrastructure is in place. The two sides finalized the field location survey for the proposed Raxaul-Kathmandu railway, agreed to cooperate on Nepal’s East-West Railway, inaugurated a bridge between Dharchula and Darchula, and made progress on several Integrated Check Posts.

The expansion of petroleum infrastructure is similarly important. The second phase of the Motihari-Amlekhgunj pipeline was inaugurated, while work was announced on a petroleum terminal in Jhapa and a prospective Siliguri-Jhapa pipeline. These are not glamorous projects, but they could improve supply reliability and reduce transport costs for a landlocked economy.

Together, these initiatives are about more than connectivity. They are also about resilience. Nepal’s reliance on a limited set of Indian transit routes has repeatedly turned logistical disruptions into wider economic and political vulnerabilities.

The 2015-16 cross-border supply disruption remains a cautionary reference point in Nepal. Many Nepalis remember it as an Indian blockade, while New Delhi attributed the disruption to protests and insecurity on the Nepali side. Whatever interpretation one adopts, the episode exposed the costs of excessive dependence on a single set of transit routes. The lesson for Kathmandu is not to resist deeper economic integration with India. It is to ensure that integration rests on predictable rules, redundant transit options, and infrastructure that can keep trade and essential supplies moving during political shocks.

Still, the new assistance package is not yet a completed outcome. The joint press release left specific projects and financing modalities to be decided in future consultations. Nepal has secured a commitment, but not yet a disbursement schedule or a detailed implementation plan.

Nepal has reason to be cautious. Earlier Indian lines of credit to Nepal, cumulatively valued at about $1.65 billion, have had a mixed implementation record. Utilization has been slowed by procurement procedures, project identification delays, and requirements to source a substantial share of materials and services from India. Some projects lacked sufficient readiness; other commitments were left underused or delayed.

This is test that Shah’s government must now meet. Kathmandu will need to identify viable projects quickly and negotiate sufficiently flexible financing terms. It will have to advance procurement and approvals without allowing the same bottlenecks to return. Finally, the Shah government should publish milestones that permit citizens to distinguish real progress from another inventory of announcements.

The implementation challenge has also plagued connectivity efforts. The Raxaul-Kathmandu railway is still in the survey stage; construction has yet to start. Access to Paradip port remains contingent on infrastructure that still needs to be built. Civil aviation gained a modest opening through a bidirectional Kathmandu-Bhairahawa-Lucknow route, but Shah’s visit did not deliver the wider operational access many Nepali stakeholders want for Gautam Buddha International Airport or a direct Delhi–Pokhara connection.

Trade issues also remain unfinished. The visit did not announce a timetable for reviewing the India-Nepal Trade Treaty, relief from safeguard duties affecting Nepali steel, mutual recognition of standards, or concrete measures to reduce delays facing Nepali agricultural exports. These steps may appear less dramatic than an infrastructure announcement, but they could have a more immediate and sustained effect on Nepali producers.

Boundary disputes involving Kalapani and Susta did not feature prominently in Indian Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri’s meetings in Nepal prior to Shah’s India trip. The joint press release from Shah’s visit noted progress in maintaining boundary pillars and directed the two foreign secretaries to continue work on outstanding boundary issues, but it offered no substantive movement on the disputes themselves. The relative absence of border disputes from the agenda helped keep the visit focused on implementable economic agreements, but it also leaves a politically sensitive issue unresolved for Shah’s government.

The treatment of the Eminent Persons Group report is especially revealing. Completed in 2018 but never formally accepted, the report has become a symbol of unresolved dissatisfaction in Nepal. Misri has suggested, however, that the Eminent Persons Group report belongs to the past and is no longer relevant to the current bilateral agenda.

Instead, Shah’s visit saw both governments commit to a “forward-looking” legal and institutional framework. The Joint Vision – titled “Viksit Bharat and Samunnat Nepal,” meaning “Developed India and Prosperous Nepal” – allows for review of existing agreements, including the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship, by mutual consent. It also provides for a High-Level Monitoring Group, led by Nepal’s foreign secretary and India’s ambassador, to meet at least every six months and report to the Joint Commission.

The High-Level Monitoring Group could matter, but only if it is more than another bilateral mechanism. Kathmandu should publish a small set of implementation milestones: project selection and financing terms for the new line of credit, construction schedules for transmission and petroleum infrastructure, progress on airport access, and measures to reduce trade and transit bottlenecks. This would offer a far better test of a forward-looking partnership than either symbolic nationalism or the repeated relitigation of the Eminent Persons Group.

Shah’s brief, business-focused visit was designed to prioritize outcomes over ceremony. He came back to Nepal with a substantial assistance commitment and a credible list of energy, transit, and connectivity projects. The question now is whether his government can do what earlier governments often could not: turn Indian commitments into projects that are financed, built, and make a difference to ordinary Nepalis.
